analysis.one_liner: Expands federal grants for preventing child and teen suicide and overdose.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, introduced December 3, 2025 with six cosponsors from both parties, sits without action in two House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends an existing grant program from the 2018 opioid law so that federal grants meant to reduce overdose deaths also cover suicide prevention among children, teens, and young adults. It adds hospitals, children's hospitals, pediatric providers, and tribal health programs to the list of groups that can receive the grants, and it funds counseling for parents and supplies to keep lethal means — like leftover drugs — away from kids. It renews the program's spending authorization through 2030, with at least $2 million per year carved out for these child-focused uses.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, adolescents, and young adults at risk of suicide or overdose, along with their families. Parents get counseling on overdose and suicide prevention and supplies to secure medications and other lethal means. Hospitals, pediatric clinics, children's hospitals, and tribal health programs become eligible for grants to run these prevention programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: At-risk kids, teens, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'suicide' to the purposes of the existing grant program, so funds can be used to prevent suicide — not only overdose — among children, adolescents, and young adults [S2].

Expands who can receive grants to include pediatric and family-medicine providers, children's hospitals, hospital emergency departments, and programs run by or under contract with the Indian Health Service [S2].
Authorizes grants, with parental consent, for counseling parents on preventing overdose and suicide and for furnishing supplies to keep lethal means away from minors [S2].
Extends the program's funding authorization from 2019–2023 to 2026–2030 and guarantees that at least $2 million of any yearly appropriation goes to these prevention grants [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through annual appropriations if Congress funds the authorization. The amounts are small — the bill guarantees at least $2 million a year to the child-focused grants but does not raise the program's overall authorized level.

drawbacks.text: Authorization is not appropriation: the bill allows spending but provides no money unless Congress passes separate appropriations each year, so the new activities could go unfunded [S2].
The bill adds new authorized spending without a stated offset or pay-for, adding to the federal deficit if fully funded [S2].
Reaching only families who volunteer and consent limits how many at-risk youth the prevention grants can touch; it does not create guaranteed services for any child [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — suicide and overdose prevention tools for families of at-risk kids — come at a modest cost to taxpayers and no cost to any industry. The main weakness is design, not intent: the bill authorizes money it cannot guarantee, and its reach depends on voluntary parental consent and on future appropriations. As a narrow expansion of an existing program, its scale is small relative to the size of youth suicide and overdose deaths.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was just introduced on December 3, 2025 and referred to two House committees — Energy and Commerce and Education and Workforce — where it awaits any action [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. John James (R-MI) introduced the bill with Reps. Debbie Dingell (D-MI), Maria Salazar (R-FL), and Angie Craig (D-MN) as original cosponsors [S2].
It was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, the Committee on Education and Workforce [S1][S4].
Six members cosponsored it — three Democrats and three Republicans — giving it bipartisan sponsorship but no committee action yet [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet; the bill is still waiting on its first committee action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill awaits committee action

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split evenly across both parties — a Republican sponsor with two Democrats and one Republican among original cosponsors, and cosponsors evenly divided 3–3 [S3].

industries.industry: Pediatric providers, children's hospitals, and hospital emergency departments
industries.note: These providers become eligible for federal prevention grants, letting them offer suicide- and overdose-prevention counseling and supplies to families. Their gain comes from delivering a service families want, not from charging patients more.

industries.industry: Tribal health programs and the Indian Health Service
industries.note: Tribes, tribal organizations, and IHS-affiliated facilities are added as eligible grant recipients, directing prevention resources to Native communities.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is two weeks old with bipartisan sponsorship but two committee referrals, which splits jurisdiction and makes floor action harder. Most bills at this stage never get a committee markup or a vote; its prospects depend on leadership scheduling and whether the SUPPORT Act reauthorization process picks it up.
